introduction: These readings think about time from the side of God. The Word of God is not a sound or a sequence of syllables; it “is sanctified beyond time,” and in the world of God “there is no past, present, or future.” When John writes “In the beginning was the Word,” ‘Abdu’l-Bahá takes “beginning” as a mark of rank and not a date: the Word was, is and will be, and its radiance varies while it does not. He draws two consequences. God’s knowing an act beforehand does not cause it, and a universe that proceeds from an eternal God has no first moment. The guide itself includes John’s prologue and two passages from Augustine’s Confessions. Beside them are the Bible’s own sayings about God and time (“I AM,” “a thousand years as yesterday,” “before Abraham was”), Plato’s definition of time, Milton on foreknowledge, Heraclitus, and Lao Tzu. The Nicene Creed reads John’s sentence of one incarnate person, Genesis has usually been read as giving the world a first day, and Khayyám speaks for everyone who feels that what is written cannot be free.
questions: “In the world of God there is no past, present, or future.” What does it do to prayer, to regret and to hope, to think of God in an eternal now?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes a beginning in time from a beginning in rank or essence. Apply the distinction to “In the beginning was the Word” and to “In the beginning God created.”
“The knowledge of a thing is not the cause of its occurrence.” Milton’s God says the same. Why does foreknowledge still feel like fate, as it does to Khayyám?
A universe without a first moment, and a God who is its cause. How can something be caused and have no beginning? Try the readings’ image of the sun and its rays.

The Word “has been from the beginning,” and yet it is heard at particular times, in particular languages, from particular persons. How do the readings relate the timeless Word to its appearances in history?

outside.why: The Word of God “is sanctified from any property or substance,” and is the cause of what has them. The Letter to the Hebrews: the worlds were framed by the word of God, so that things which are seen were not made of things which do appear.
A psalm: he spake, and it was done; he commanded, and it stood fast.
“In the world of God there is no past, present, or future.” A psalm: from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God; a thousand years in thy sight are but as yesterday when it is past.
The Name given to Moses is in the present tense: I AM THAT I AM.
Verses received “limitless beyond reckoning by century, age, epoch.” Isaiah: the word of our God shall stand for ever.
The reality of prophethood “has neither beginning nor end.” Jesus, with a present tense where the past was expected: before Abraham was, I am.
Wisdom speaks in Proverbs as present before creation: when he prepared the heavens, I was there.
“Its radiance varies like that of the sun,” while it does not. The Letter to the Hebrews: Jesus Christ the same yesterday, and to day, and for ever.
Revelation: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá reads “In the beginning was the Word” of a reality that shines in every Manifestation. The creed reads it of one person: begotten of the Father before all worlds, and for our salvation incarnate once. What is gained and what is given up by each reading of John’s first sentence?
“Yesterday, today and tomorrow do not exist” in relation to God. The Second Letter of Peter: one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.
The Qur’án: a Day with Allah is as a thousand years of what ye reckon.
Time and place “are relative matters,” belonging to this earth. Plato’s Timaeus: he resolved to have a moving image of eternity, and this image we call time.
What is revealed today “has been that Divine Word” from before. Jesus: heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away.

Everything will be seized by extinction “save the Sun of the Word of God.” Ecclesiastes sets the two side by side: he hath made every thing beautiful in his time; also he hath set the world in their heart.

“The knowledge of a thing is not the cause of its occurrence.” Milton gives God the same defence: if I foreknew, foreknowledge had no influence on their fault, which had no less proved certain unforeknown.

An act written in the Guarded Tablet can still be the actor’s own. FitzGerald’s Khayyám could not feel it so: the Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, moves on: nor all your piety nor wit shall lure it back to cancel half a line. What picture of time makes foreknowledge feel like compulsion, and what picture do the readings offer in its place?

“The first thing to emanate from God” is the Primal Will, without beginning in time. Lao Tzu orders things in a like sequence: the Tao produced One; One produced Two; Two produced Three; Three produced All things.
Since God is eternal, “this endless universe … has no beginning.” Heraclitus: this world was ever, is now, and ever shall be an ever-living Fire.

A universe without beginning. The first sentence of the Bible has been read for centuries as fixing one: in the beginning God created the heaven and the earth. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks elsewhere of an “essential” beginning as distinct from a beginning in time. Can Genesis bear that reading?

The oldest hymn of India ends its account of creation with a question: who verily knows whence it first came into being? He, the first origin of this creation, he verily knows it, or perhaps he knows not. What kind of answer do the readings give: a history, or a relation?
“In the presence of God … there is an eternal now.” Isaiah: the high and lofty One that inhabiteth eternity, whose name is Holy.
